For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. For $\Lambda=\varnothing$, $S_\Lambda$ is a singleton and $\mathcal H_\Lambda\cong\mathbb C$. The **local spin matrix algebra** is

$$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

derivations.claim:
Let $s\ne t$ in $S_{\mathrm{fin}}$. They differ at some site $x$; set $a=s_x$ and $Q:=\pi(E_x^{aa})$. Then $Qe_s=e_s$ and $Qe_t=0$. Since $TQ=QT$, self-adjointness of $Q$ gives
$$\langle Te_s,e_t\rangle=\langle QTe_s,e_t\rangle=\langle Te_s,Qe_t\rangle=0.$$
Thus every off-diagonal coefficient of $Te_s$ vanishes, so completeness of the specified orthonormal basis implies $Te_s=c_s e_s$ for some scalar $c_s$. The representation and completion are under the exact Countable Choice hypothesis A1.

If two configurations $s,t$ differ at only one site $x$, choose the matrix unit $E_x^{t_xs_x}$. By [F2], $\pi(E_x^{t_xs_x})e_s=e_t$. Commuting this operator through $T$ gives $c_t e_t=T e_t=T\pi(E_x^{t_xs_x})e_s=\pi(E_x^{t_xs_x})T e_s=c_s e_t$, hence $c_t=c_s$. Any $s,t\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}$ differ on a finite set, and changing those finitely many labels one site at a time connects them; therefore all $c_s$ equal a single scalar $c$.

Step 2.1 proves every $T$ in the commutant is $cI$, while scalars commute with all operators, so $\pi(\mathcal A)'=\mathbb C I$. The definition of bicommutant then gives $\pi(\mathcal A)''=(\mathbb C I)'=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{vac}})$. Faithfulness follows from the isometry established in [[def-qsm-vacuum-spin-representation]].

derivations.claim: The finite Hermitian spectral calculus [F11] diagonalizes $h$ with real eigenvalues; exponentiating them gives $Z>0$ and a positive trace-one matrix $r$. For nested finite regions $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, the product-basis trace factorization and $\operatorname{Tr}r=1$ give $\operatorname{Tr}_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}(r^{\otimes\Lambda'})=r^{\otimes\Lambda}$. Thus the family is consistent, and [F5] defines a unique state $\omega_r$ with the displayed local restrictions.

Let $\Lambda_n=[-n,n]^d\cap\Gamma$. In a finite-volume product eigenbasis, $H_{\Lambda_n}=\sum_{x\in\Lambda_n}h_x$ has eigenvalues equal to sums of the corresponding one-site eigenvalues by [F11]. Therefore $e^{-\beta H_{\Lambda_n}}=(e^{-\beta h})^{\otimes\Lambda_n}$ and its partition function is $Z^{|\Lambda_n|}$, so its normalized Gibbs density is $r^{\otimes\Lambda_n}$. For every finite $X\subseteq\Gamma$, define $$\rho_X^{(n)}:=\operatorname{Tr}_{(X\cup\Lambda_n)\setminus X}\!\left(r^{\otimes\Lambda_n}\otimes(q^{-1}I)^{\otimes(X\setminus\Lambda_n)}\right),$$ placing the tensor factors on $\Lambda_n$ and $X\setminus\Lambda_n$ respectively. These densities are consistent: removing a site outside $\Lambda_n$ traces a factor $q^{-1}I$ to $1$, while tracing sites in $\Lambda_n$ commutes with the displayed partial trace because both are finite tensor-basis sums. Therefore [F5] gives an algebraic state $\omega_n$ on $\mathcal A$. If $A$ is local in $\mathcal A_X$, then for all sufficiently large $n$, $X\subseteq\Lambda_n$ and $\omega_n(A)=\omega_r(A)$. For arbitrary $A\in\mathcal A$, choose local $C$ with $\|A-C\|<\varepsilon/4$ using [F2]; since both states have norm one, $|\omega_n(A)-\omega_r(A)|\le2\|A-C\|+|\omega_n(C)-\omega_r(C)|<\varepsilon$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Hence $\omega_n\to\omega_r$ pointwise on $\mathcal A$.

Applying the local-pair conclusion of [F7] to this particular pointwise-convergent finite Gibbs sequence gives, for every local $C,D$, a bounded continuous strip function $F_{C,D}$, holomorphic inside, with lower and upper edges $\omega_r(C\alpha_t(D))$ and $\omega_r(\alpha_t(D)C)$. This is precisely the local conclusion of [F7]; no whole-algebra KMS conclusion is attributed to that supplier.

Let $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and choose local sequences $A_n\to A$, $B_n\to B$. On either boundary, the correlation difference for local pairs is bounded by $$\|A_n-A_m\|\,\|B_n\|+\|A_m\|\,\|B_n-B_m\|,$$ because $\omega_r$ has norm one and $\alpha_t$ is isometric by [F4]. Decomposing the difference into the two local-pair differences $(A_n-A_m,B_n)$ and $(A_m,B_n-B_m)$, [F8] gives the same bound throughout the strip; its zero-edge uniqueness makes this decomposition equal to $F_{A_n,B_n}-F_{A_m,B_m}$. The right side tends to zero, since the convergent sequences have bounded norms. Thus $F_{A_n,B_n}$ is uniformly Cauchy on the closed strip. Its limit $F_{A,B}$ is bounded and continuous there and is holomorphic inside by [F10]. Norm continuity of $\omega_r$, $\alpha_t$, and multiplication gives the required lower and upper boundary values. Therefore $\omega_r$ is KMS for all $A,B\in\mathcal A$.

derivations.claim: For $s\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}$ and finite $F\subseteq\Gamma$, let $P_F^s\in\mathcal A_F$ be the projection onto the one-dimensional local basis vector with configuration $s|_F$. If $t\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}$, then $\pi(P_F^s)e_t=e_t$ exactly when $t|_F=s|_F$, and otherwise it is zero. Thus, as $F$ increases over finite subsets ordered by inclusion, $\pi(P_F^s)$ decreases strongly to the rank-one projection $E_s:=|e_s\rangle\langle e_s|$: each basis vector $e_t$ with $t\ne s$ eventually fails at a site where it differs from $s$, and $e_s$ remains fixed. Since all these projections have norm at most one and the finite span of the basis is dense, convergence on basis vectors extends to strong convergence on every vector.

Let $k_s:=|\{x:s_x\ne0\}|$. Once $F$ contains this finite support, the product-state expectation is
$$\omega_r(P_F^s)=\prod_{x\in F}\langle s_x,r s_x\rangle=\left(\prod_{x:s_x\ne0}\langle s_x,r s_x\rangle\right)p_0^{\,|F|-k_s}.$$
Because $0<p_0<1$ and $\Gamma$ is infinite, this tends to zero along the directed set of finite regions: for every $N$ all sufficiently large $F$ have $|F|-k_s\ge N$.

Suppose a normal state $\widetilde\omega$ on $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_{\mathrm{vac}})$ extended $\omega_r$. The complements $Q_F:=I-\pi(P_F^s)$ are increasing projections. The projection onto the closure of the union of their increasing ranges is their least upper bound: it dominates each $Q_F$, and any upper bound dominates that closed span. Strong convergence in step 1.1 identifies this supremum as $I-E_s$. Normality and step 1.2 give
$$\widetilde\omega(I-E_s)=\sup_F\widetilde\omega(I-\pi(P_F^s))=\sup_F\bigl(1-\omega_r(P_F^s)\bigr)=1,$$
so $\widetilde\omega(E_s)=0$ for every $s\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}$. For finite $J\subseteq S_{\mathrm{fin}}$, the projections $R_J:=\sum_{s\in J}E_s$ increase to $I$ as $J$ ranges over finite subsets, because $(e_s)$ is a complete orthonormal basis. Applying normality again gives
$$1=\widetilde\omega(I)=\sup_J\widetilde\omega(R_J)=0,$$
a contradiction. Therefore no normal extension exists.

Suppose instead a positive trace-class density $\rho$ represented an extension. By [F4], for each $s$ and finite $F$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\pi(P_F^s))=\sum_j\lambda_j\langle\pi(P_F^s)u_j,u_j\rangle.$$
For every fixed $N$, strong convergence in step 1.1 makes the first $N$ terms converge to $\sum_{j\le N}\lambda_j\langle E_su_j,u_j\rangle$. The tails of both the $\pi(P_F^s)$ sum and its proposed $E_s$ limit are bounded by $\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j$, because each operator is a projection. Hence their tail difference is at most $2\sum_{j>N}\lambda_j$, which tends to zero; therefore $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\pi(P_F^s))\to\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_s)$. Step 1.2 then gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho E_s)=0$ for each $s$. The same finite-tail argument applied to $R_J\uparrow I$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho I)=\sup_J\operatorname{Tr}(\rho R_J)=0$, contradicting $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$. Thus no such trace-class density exists.

derivations.claim: By the specified onsite-only interaction, $H_\Lambda=0$ for every finite $\Lambda$, so each finite-volume dynamics is the identity and its thermodynamic limit is $\alpha_t=\mathrm{id}$. Hence $\omega_0(\alpha_t(A))=\omega_0(A)$ for every $A$ and $t$, so $\omega_0$ is stationary. The vector formula is a normalized positive state because $\pi$ is a unital $*$-representation and $\|\Omega\|=1.
At any site $x$, set $A=E_x^{01}$ and $B=E_x^{10}$. Then $AB=E_x^{00}$ and $BA=E_x^{11}$, so $\omega_0(AB)=1$ and $\omega_0(BA)=0$. Therefore $\omega_0$ is not tracial.

If $\omega_0$ were $\beta$-KMS, its correlation function for this pair would have the constant lower boundary $F(t)=1$. The constant function $G(z)=1$ is bounded, continuous and holomorphic on the strip with the same lower edge; [F4] forces $F=G$ throughout, so its upper edge at $t=0$ would also be $1$. But the KMS upper edge equals $\omega_0(BA)=0$, a contradiction. Hence this stationary state is not $\beta$-KMS for any $\beta>0$.

By [F5], the unique $\beta$-KMS state of this zero-Hamiltonian model is the tracial product state with one-site density $q^{-1}I$, which differs from $\omega_0$. The counterexample distinguishes stationarity from thermal equilibrium without asserting that every stationary state fails KMS.

For $n\in\mathbb Z$, define $|n|=n$ if $0\le n$ and $|n|=-n$ if $n<0$, using the integer order and additive inverse of [[def-int-order]] and [[def-int-operations]]. Totality and compatibility of the integer order with addition ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]]) give $0\le|n|$ and $-|n|\le n\le|n|$. Adding these bounds for $m,n\in\mathbb Z$ gives $|m+n|\le|m|+|n|$. Equip $\Gamma$ with the max-coordinate metric $d_\infty(x,y)=\max_{1\le r\le d}|x_r-y_r|$; the maximum exists because the coordinate set is finite and nonempty, symmetry and separation hold coordinatewise, and the absolute-value triangle inequality gives $|x_r-z_r|\le|x_r-y_r|+|y_r-z_r|$ for every coordinate, hence the triangle inequality for $d_\infty$. A **finite region** is a finite subset $\Lambda\subseteq\Gamma$; its cardinality is $|\Lambda|$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]).

For a finite region $\Lambda$, let $S_\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,q\}^{\Lambda}$ be the set of spin configurations on $\Lambda$. Induction on $|\Lambda|$ gives $|S_\Lambda|=q^{|\Lambda|}$: the empty region has one configuration, and for $x\in\Lambda$ the restriction map $s\mapsto(s|_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}},s(x))$ is a bijection $S_\Lambda\to S_{\Lambda\setminus\{x\}}\times\{1,\ldots,q\}$, so adjoining one site multiplies the number of configurations by $q$, according to the recursion defining natural-number powers in [[def-nat-power]]. Let $\mathcal H_\Lambda$ be the vector space of functions $f:S_\Lambda\to\mathbb C$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}f(s)\overline{g(s)}$. For each $s\in S_\Lambda$, let $e_s$ be the indicator function of $\{s\}$; these vectors form an orthonormal basis. $$\mathcal A_\Lambda:=\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)\cong M_{q^{|\Lambda|}}(\mathbb C),$$

Here $\mathcal B(\mathcal H_\Lambda)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms of the finite-dimensional Hilbert space; they are bounded. The algebra has composition, Hilbert adjoint, identity $I_\Lambda$, and induced operator norm

$$\|T\|:=\sup_{\|\xi\|=1}\|T\xi\|.$$

The **finite local trace** is $\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(T):=\sum_{s\in S_\Lambda}\langle T e_s,e_s\rangle$ in the displayed configuration basis $(e_s)$. This is the usual finite-matrix trace; basis independence and its cyclic/unitary identities are supplied by [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]].

If $\Lambda\subseteq\Lambda'$, restriction of configurations gives the canonical factorization $\mathcal H_{\Lambda'}\cong\mathcal H_\Lambda\otimes\mathcal H_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$, with sites ordered lexicographically. The **factor inclusion** is the unital $*$-homomorphism $\iota_{\Lambda,\Lambda'}:\mathcal A_\Lambda\to\mathcal A_{\Lambda'}$ given by $T\mapsto T\otimes I_{\Lambda'\setminus\Lambda}$. Together with Countable Choice [A1], $h=0=h^*$, $\beta>0$ and $\hbar>0$, these meet its hypotheses. Since $e^{-\beta h}=I$ and $\operatorname{Tr}I=q$, the density is $r=q^{-1}I$, so $r^{\otimes\Lambda}=q^{-|\Lambda|}I_\Lambda$, and [F1] identifies its extension as the unique $\beta$-KMS state.

If $A,B$ are local, embed them into a common finite region $\Lambda$ using [F3]. Then $$\omega(AB)=q^{-|\Lambda|}\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(AB)=q^{-|\Lambda|}\operatorname{Tr}_\Lambda(BA)=\omega(BA),$$ by finite-matrix trace cyclicity.

$$\|A_nB_n-AB\|\le\|A_n-A\|\,\|B_n\|+\|A\|\,\|B_n-B\|\longrightarrow0,$$
with the same estimate after exchanging $A_n,B_n$ and $A,B$. Boundedness of the state then gives $\omega(A_nB_n)\to\omega(AB)$ and $\omega(B_nA_n)\to\omega(BA)$. Step 2.1 gives equality at each $n$, so $\omega(AB)=\omega(BA)$; the state is tracial on the full algebra.
